opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's worth being careful about what we mean by "diminishing returns," because the phrase gets used in a couple of different ways that point in quite different directions.

In one sense, diminishing returns are built into how we've understood scaling from the start. The scaling laws people have estimated describe loss falling as a power law in compute. So if you want the same absolute reduction in loss, you need multiplicatively more compute each time, perhaps ten times more for each step. In that narrow sense, returns are diminishing, and they always have been. That isn't new and it isn't a sign that anything is breaking.

The more interesting question is whether that matters for what we actually care about, which is capabilities and economic value. Here I think the answer is much less obvious. Loss is a fairly abstract quantity. Small reductions in loss near the frontier can correspond to quite large jumps in what a model can do: whether it can reliably carry out a multi-step task, write working code, or reason through a problem without falling apart halfway. The relationship between loss and usefulness isn't linear. So you can have diminishing returns in loss and still get increasing, or at least steady, returns in capabilities that matter.

The second point is that the cost side has been changing too. The relevant input isn't really raw compute but effective compute: hardware getting cheaper per FLOP, plus algorithmic progress that lets you get the same performance with less compute. Historically, algorithmic efficiency has improved quite rapidly. So even if each order of magnitude buys you a bit less, the price of an order of magnitude keeps falling. Whether the overall picture looks like diminishing returns depends on the race between those two things.

Third, what you get from compute also depends on how you spend it. A few years ago the story was mostly pretraining: bigger models, more data. Now there's much more weight on post-training, reinforcement learning, and inference-time compute, where you let models think longer or try several approaches. These open new axes along which you can scale. If one axis starts to saturate, you can shift to another. Treating "compute scaling" as a single curve that's either bending or not misses that.

So where would I expect real diminishing returns to bite? I'd look more at the inputs than at some intrinsic ceiling in the learning process. Data is one candidate: high-quality human-generated text is finite, though synthetic data and RL environments may relax that. Then there are the physical and economic constraints: chip production, power, the willingness of investors to fund ever-larger training runs. Those seem to me more likely to slow things down than the scaling curves themselves flattening out.

And the key consideration, from my perspective, is that if AI systems become capable enough to contribute to AI research and to the broader economy, you get feedback loops. More capable systems generate more value, which funds more compute, and they might also speed up algorithmic progress directly. In that world, modest diminishing returns at the level of any single training run could be overwhelmed by accelerating returns at the level of the whole system. That's why I'm skeptical of arguments that go "returns are diminishing, therefore progress will stall." You have to model the whole loop, not just one curve.

r001.rationale: The response says loss follows a power law in compute and that each equal-sized loss reduction requires multiplicatively more compute. It does not say each compute doubling yields approximately the same absolute performance gain.

r002.rationale: The response does not connect exponential growth in training compute over time to linear performance improvement over time.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that "diminishing returns" is a phrase that gets used in a few different ways, and it's worth separating them out, because some of them are true and fairly uninteresting, and some of them are the actual crux.

The uninteresting sense is just that, if you look at a scaling law, loss falls as a power law in compute. So each additional unit of compute buys you less reduction in loss than the previous unit did. That's been true since the very first scaling papers, it's baked into the functional form, and nobody who works on this thinks it's news. In that sense, yes, there are diminishing returns, and there always have been.

But I think the question people actually care about is something like: do the marginal gains from scaling, measured in terms of capabilities we care about, fall off fast enough that it stops being worth pouring resources in? And there the picture is more subtle, for a couple of reasons.

One is that the relationship between loss and downstream capability is not linear, and often not even smooth. You can get fairly modest, boring-looking improvements in pretraining loss that correspond to a model crossing some threshold where it can now do multi-step reasoning, or write working code, or whatever. So looking at the loss curve and concluding returns are diminishing can be misleading about what's happening on the things that actually generate economic value.

The second is that compute is really the input you should be measuring against, not model size or data alone. When we've looked at this at Epoch, training compute for frontier models has been growing something like four to five times per year. The reason that's sustainable despite the power-law form is that the inputs are getting cheaper. Hardware price-performance improves, algorithmic efficiency improves, so the effective compute you can buy per dollar keeps going up. Our estimates suggest algorithmic progress alone has been worth something like a doubling of effective compute every eight months or so. So diminishing returns in the physical compute sense are being offset by the fact that you need less of it to get the same result.

Then I think the deeper question, the one I spend more time on, is whether the returns diminish in an economic sense. If you think about compute as a factor of production, the relevant thing is the elasticity: if I double compute, by how much does output increase? A lot of the standard growth models that people use to be skeptical about AI have the elasticity falling over time, so eventually scaling stops paying for itself. But there's a reasonable argument that if AI systems start substituting for human cognitive labor, then the returns to compute look much more like the returns to adding workers, which historically have not diminished in the way people expected, because you get complementarities, you get the ability to tackle new problems. So the answer to "are there diminishing returns" depends heavily on what you think the compute is actually buying you.

My honest view is that we're not yet seeing evidence of returns flattening in a way that would change the trajectory. The binding constraints I'd worry about are more practical: can you actually get the power, the chips, the data at the scale required, rather than the scaling relationship itself breaking down. But I hold that view with uncertainty, and I'd update if we started seeing frontier labs train much bigger models and get little out of it.

r001.rationale: The response describes loss falling as a power law, with each additional unit of compute buying less loss reduction. It does not say each compute doubling yields approximately the same absolute performance gain.

r002.rationale: It reports that frontier training compute has grown roughly four to five times per year, but does not explain that this implies linear performance improvement over time under a log-linear relationship.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish diminishing returns in prediction loss from diminishing returns in capabilities or economic value. Those aren’t necessarily the same thing.

When we scale training compute, we tend to see something like a power-law improvement in loss. That means each additional unit of compute buys you a smaller absolute improvement. To keep making comparable proportional improvements, you need to increase compute by a multiplicative factor rather than simply adding a fixed amount.

But loss measures how well a model predicts its training distribution. It doesn’t directly measure how useful that model is. A relatively small improvement in prediction can make the difference between a system that’s unreliable at a task and one that’s reliable enough to use. So you could have diminishing returns in loss while still seeing substantial improvements in useful capabilities.

The question, then, is whether those improvements justify the growing cost of training and deploying the models. Diminishing returns alone don’t tell us that scaling is about to stop working. They tell us that progress gets more expensive, holding other things fixed. Algorithmic improvements and better use of data can change that tradeoff.

r001.rationale: The response describes power-law improvements in loss, with smaller absolute gains from additional compute; it does not say each compute doubling yields roughly the same absolute performance gain.

r002.rationale: It says comparable proportional improvements require multiplicative compute increases, but does not explain that exponential compute growth yields linear performance improvement over time.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish diminishing returns in the loss from diminishing returns in capabilities or economic value. Those aren’t necessarily the same thing.

When we scale up compute, we generally see the loss—the model’s prediction error—fall according to something like a power law. So each additional unit of compute buys you a smaller absolute reduction in loss. In that sense, there are diminishing returns, and you need multiplicative increases in compute to keep making progress.

But that doesn’t tell you directly how useful the resulting system is. A relatively small improvement in prediction could make the difference between a model that can almost do a task and one that can do it reliably. That can be a substantial increase in value, even if the improvement in loss looks modest.

So I’d be cautious about going from ‘there are diminishing returns to compute on this training metric’ to ‘scaling is about to stop producing meaningful improvements.’ To assess that, you need to understand how those improvements translate into capabilities, reliability, and ultimately the tasks people want these systems to perform.

r001.rationale: The response describes loss falling by a power law, with smaller absolute reductions as compute increases. It does not say that each doubling of compute yields approximately the same absolute performance gain.

r002.rationale: The response does not explain that exponential compute growth implies linear performance improvement over time under a log-linear relationship.
